claim: Average hourly earnings on online web-based platforms are US$3.4 once unpaid time is counted, half of workers earn less than US$2.1 an hour, and 66 per cent earn below the average.
stance_target: The position that platform-mediated online earnings are right-skewed and that most workers fall below the widely-quoted average
scope_conditions: Global; n = 4,009 pooled (about 2,900 respondents from 100 countries in ILO global microtask 2017 and freelance/competitive programming 2019-20 surveys, plus China n=1,107 and Ukraine n=761, both 2019); microtask and freelance platforms, NOT content creation; non-probability convenience sample of active workers; data trimmed at the 1st and 99th percentile by sector
quoted_support: Average hourly earnings in a typical week for those engaged on online web-based platforms are US$3.4, while half of the workers on these platforms earn less than US$2.1 per hour.

claim: Counting unpaid time for searching, bidding and profile-building cuts platform hourly earnings roughly by a third: from US$11.2 to US$7.6 on freelance platforms and from US$4.4 to US$3.3 on microtask platforms.
stance_target: The position that headline platform and creator hourly rates are overstated because unpaid preparation and search labour is excluded
scope_conditions: Global; ILO surveys 2017-2020, n = 4,009; freelance and microtask platforms; unpaid time defined as looking for work and building up a profile; non-probability sample
quoted_support: On freelance platforms, when unpaid time is accounted for, the total average hourly earnings (paid and unpaid) drop to US$7.6, with 64 per cent earning below the average.

claim: Between 15 and 19 per cent of app-based platform workers have had their account deactivated, and for 7 to 15 per cent of those the deactivation was permanent, an involuntary exit mechanism with no equivalent in voluntary-quit survey data.
stance_target: The position that platform attrition is partly involuntary and algorithmically imposed, not solely a matter of workers choosing to quit
scope_conditions: App-based taxi (9 countries) and delivery (11 countries) sectors, about 5,000 respondents, 2019-20; location-based gig work, NOT content creation; the ILO notes that permanently deactivated workers were reached only because they had moved to another platform, so fully-exited workers are absent from the sample
quoted_support: deactivation lasted for up to seven days for the majority in both the taxi (73 per cent) and delivery (69 per cent) sectors, while it was permanent for some (7 and 15 per cent respectively).
numbers: 73 per cent up to seven days (taxi)
69 per cent up to seven days (delivery)
region: 9-11 countries across Arab States, Africa, Asia and the Pacific, Eastern Europe, Latin America

claim: The binding constraint on platform earnings is demand, not effort: about 45 per cent of workers who want more work cite lack of available work, 41 per cent on freelance platforms cite difficulty finding clients, and 18 per cent on microtask platforms cite inability to find well-paid tasks.
stance_target: The position that platform and creator income ceilings are set by demand scarcity and oversupply rather than by individual productivity
scope_conditions: Global; ILO online web-based platform surveys 2017-2020; figures refer only to the subset of workers who said they would like to undertake more online work; non-probability sample
quoted_support: One key factor preventing people from doing more work on online web-based platforms is lack of availability of sufficient work. About 45 per cent of respondents reported this to be the case.
numbers: 45 per cent lack of available work

claim: Every ILO platform-worker earnings statistic comes from a non-probability convenience sample of currently-active workers, because no sampling frame for platform workers exists.
stance_target: The position that survivorship bias is unavoidable in platform and creator income research and must be flagged on every derived figure
scope_conditions: Global; applies to all ILO platform-worker surveys 2017-2020; the caveat is stated by the ILO about its own data
quoted_support: Given the lack of official statistical information on the numbers and characteristics of platform workers... there was no sampling base from which a random sample could be drawn.

claim: Microtask platform workers earn 64 per cent less in India and 81 per cent less in the United States than people doing comparable work in the traditional labour market, after controlling for basic characteristics.
stance_target: The claim that platform-mediated digital work pays at least as well as equivalent conventional employment
scope_conditions: India and United States; ILO global crowdworker survey 2017 compared against India NSSO Periodic Labour Force Survey 2017-18 and US comparison data; microtask platforms only; the gap is wider for female workers in both countries
quoted_support: Microtask workers earn 64 per cent less in India, and 81 per cent less in the United States than in the traditional labour market.
numbers: 60 per cent developing-country discount on freelance platforms

claim: The ILO finds no global gender pay gap in hourly earnings on freelance platforms once education and experience are controlled for, though significant gaps persist at country level, which is more equivocal than the secondary literature that cites it.
stance_target: The claim that platform work carries a uniform global gender pay gap
scope_conditions: Global; ILO freelance-platform surveys 2019-20; controls for education level and work experience; country-level gaps still found on both online and location-based platforms
quoted_support: After controlling for basic characteristics, such as education level and work experience, at the global level there is no difference in hourly earnings, while at the country level there is a significant gender pay gap in some cases.
